title: One Source Metal Prescribed T661 Forms (July 2009 TCC)
subject: SR&ED appeal concerning the mandatory requirement to file prescribed Form T661 within the statutory 18-month deadline.
keyPhrase: One Source Metal T661 forms 2009 TCC
summary: One Source Metal (2009 TCC 511) shows how strictly subsection 37(11) of the Income Tax Act governs Canadian SR&ED claims: the Tax Court of Canada denied a corporate claimant's 2005 SR&ED deduction because it could not prove its technical report was filed with its T661 forms by the 12-month reporting deadline of March 31, 2007.
metaDescription: Review the July 2009 Tax Court of Canada ruling for One Source Metal on the mandatory use of prescribed T661 forms for SR&ED.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background

The decision of the Tax Court of Canada in 1373744 Ontario Inc. o/a One Source Metal v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2009 TCC 511 (Docket: 2008-3566(IT)I), heard on July 8, 2009, in Toronto, Ontario, by the Honourable Justice E.A. Bowie, with formal judgment and Reasons for Judgment signed at Ottawa on October 14, 2009, stands as an instructive illustration (though, having been decided under the Informal Procedure, it has no precedential value pursuant to section 18.28 of the Tax Court of Canada Act) of procedural compliance and the evidentiary burden of proof under Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program. While substantive SR&ED litigation before the Tax Court of Canada frequently centres on whether a claimant's shop-floor or laboratory activities satisfy the statutory definition of systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, One Source Metal illustrates the unforgiving threshold operation of subsection 37(11) of the Canadian Income Tax Act (ITA). The ruling illustrates that a claimed SR&ED expenditure deduction (the only matter before the Court—the Reasons address neither the Investment Tax Credit (ITC) nor the merits of the underlying work) will be denied if the taxpayer fails to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that every component of the claim that, as was common ground between the parties, had to be filed—here, both the T661 (with Schedule 31 and Schedule 1) and the technical report—was filed with the Minister of National Revenue on or before the statutory 12-month reporting deadline.
Summary of the Taxpayer's Claim and Factual Chronology

The Appellant, 1373744 Ontario Inc., carrying on business under the operating name One Source Metal, appealed from an income tax reassessment issued by the Minister of National Revenue under the Income Tax Act for its 2005 taxation year. Specifically, the appeal challenged the Minister's complete disallowance of the Appellant's claimed deduction for SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the ITA. Although the Reasons for Judgment do not state the Appellant's fiscal year-end, the agreed March 31, 2007 deadline is consistent with a fiscal year ending September 30, 2005, and a corporate income tax return (T2) filing-due date pursuant to paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA of March 31, 2006. Under subsection 37(11) of the ITA, which grants a taxpayer exactly 12 months following its income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year to submit its prescribed SR&ED forms, it was common ground between the Appellant and the Crown that the statutory deadline for filing a compliant 2005 SR&ED claim expired on March 31, 2007. Both parties further agreed that statutory compliance with subsection 37(11) for the 2005 taxation year required that two distinct documentary elements be filed with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) before the end of March 2007: first, Form T661 (referred to in the Reasons as the "T-661") accompanied by Schedule 31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) and Schedule 1, and second, the technical report describing the underlying SR&ED projects.

To prepare its SR&ED claims for both the 2005 and 2006 taxation years, the Appellant divided professional responsibilities between two separate external advisory firms. The technical report, which was common to the 2005 and 2006 taxation years, was prepared by a firm called Business Improvement Group which, according to the Reasons, had also done the work giving rise to the claims (the Reasons do not describe it as a specialized SR&ED consulting firm). Concurrently, the Appellant engaged an external accounting firm, Martyn, Dooley and Partners, LLP, where staff accountant Kevin Wong was responsible for preparing the financial tax forms, specifically the T661 forms accompanied by Schedule 31 and Schedule 1 for both the 2005 and 2006 taxation years.

On March 27, 2007—just four days prior to the statutory bar date for the 2005 claim—Benjamin Mair, the principal of One Source Metal, attended the offices of Martyn, Dooley and Partners, LLP, signed the 2005 and 2006 claim documents, and left the executed documents with the accountants to be filed with the CRA. Mr. Mair had no personal involvement in, or direct knowledge of, the subsequent physical delivery of those documents to the tax authorities. According to the testimony of Mr. Wong, after receiving the consolidated technical report from Business Improvement Group, he assembled the submission package by stapling the 2005 Form T661 and its accompanying schedules into one unit, stapling the 2006 Form T661 and its schedules into a second unit, and stapling the pages of the technical report together into a third separate unit. Rather than enclosing the filing package inside a sealed envelope or binding the technical narrative directly into each respective annual Form T661, Mr. Wong joined the three separately stapled documents together using a single paper clip. He prepared two sets of these documents—one stamped "federal copy" for retention by the CRA and a duplicate set stamped "file copy" to be date-stamped by the CRA counter clerk upon delivery as proof of filing.

On March 28, 2007, Blair Mabee, an employee of Martyn, Dooley and Partners, LLP, took the documents given to him by Mr. Wong and hand-delivered them to the CRA's Toronto West Tax Services Office. While the Appellant contended at trial that all three stapled documents—the 2005 T661 package, the 2006 T661 package, and the shared technical report—were paper-clipped together and filed at the Toronto West Tax Services Office on March 28, 2007, the Respondent maintained that the technical report was missing at the time of filing and was only transmitted to the CRA via facsimile on April 12, 2007, after the statutory deadline had passed.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

Following the March 28, 2007 counter submission at the Toronto West Tax Services Office, the Appellant's SR&ED claim would, according to the evidence of CRA appeals officer Christine Lockwood that all SR&ED claims are sent to Sudbury immediately upon filing, have been sent to the CRA's Sudbury office to be logged and evaluated. On April 10, 2007—ten days after the March 31, 2007 statutory deadline had expired—a CRA assessor telephoned the Appellant's representative to notify them that the technical report was missing from the submitted T661 forms. According to the Respondent, the technical report was first filed with the CRA in the form of a fax sent and received on April 12, 2007, and the Ontario Revenue Department's records showed that the technical report had been filed with the provincial authority on April 13, 2007.

The Minister of National Revenue reassessed the Appellant for the 2005 taxation year to deny the claimed SR&ED expenditure deduction in its entirety. Represented by Crown counsel Jenna Clark and student-at-law Ariane Asselin (acting for John H. Sims, Q.C., Deputy Attorney General of Canada), the Respondent challenged the Appellant's claim strictly on the statutory mandate of subsection 37(11) of the ITA. Because it was common ground that compliance with subsection 37(11) for 2005 required that both the T661 and the technical report be filed before the end of March 2007, and because, in the Respondent's view, the technical report was not filed with the Minister until April 12, 2007, the Respondent asserted that the claim was not filed within the time limited by the Act (the Reasons do not themselves characterize the technical report as "prescribed information"; the filing requirement was common ground). The Reasons do not address the 2006 taxation year, which was not before the Court; the appeal concerned only the 2005 taxation year, for which the absence of the technical report prior to March 31, 2007, was fatal.
Governing Canadian Statutory Framework

The statutory framework governing One Source Metal is rooted in section 37 (and, for the Investment Tax Credit, subsection 127(9)) of the Canadian Income Tax Act—although the Reasons for Judgment quote and apply only subsection 37(11)—which establish a two-tiered architecture linking substantive expenditure deductibility and tax credit generation to strict procedural disclosure deadlines. Subsection 37(1) of the ITA establishes the substantive pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures, permitting a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to deduct current expenditures (and, during applicable statutory periods, capital expenditures) incurred on scientific research and experimental development carried on in Canada, directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer, and related to a business of the taxpayer.

Entitlement to deduct any amount under subsection 37(1), however, is expressly conditioned upon compliance with subsection 37(11) of the ITA. As quoted by Justice Bowie in paragraph 2 of the Reasons for Judgment, subsection 37(11) stipulates that, subject to subsection 37(12), no amount in respect of an expenditure that would be incurred by a taxpayer in a taxation year that begins after 1995 (if the Act were read without reference to subsection 78(4)) may be deducted under subsection 37(1) unless the taxpayer files with the Minister a prescribed form containing prescribed information in respect of the expenditure on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the year. Because a corporation's income tax return filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) of the ITA is six months after the end of its taxation year (as defined in subsection 249(1)), a corporate claimant has a total non-extendable window of 18 months following its fiscal year-end to file the prescribed SR&ED forms.

The legal consequences of failing to satisfy subsection 37(11) are codified in subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12) of the ITA (neither of which is referred to in the Reasons in One Source Metal; subsection 37(11.1) was added to the Act after the decision, and the version of subsection 37(11) quoted by Justice Bowie contains no paragraphs (a) and (b)). Under subsection 37(11.1), subject to subsection 37(12), if the prescribed information in respect of an expenditure referred to in paragraph 37(11)(a) is not contained in the prescribed form referred to in subsection 37(11), no amount in respect of the expenditure may be deducted under subsection 37(1). Subsection 37(12) then imposes a conclusive statutory deeming rule: if a taxpayer has not filed a prescribed form in respect of an expenditure in accordance with subsection 37(11), for the purposes of the Income Tax Act, the expenditure is deemed not to be an expenditure on or in respect of scientific research and experimental development. Consequently, missing the 12-month reporting deadline—or filing a form that omits mandatory prescribed information—does not merely trigger an administrative penalty or reduce the claim; it alters the substantive legal character of the expenditure, precluding both pool deductibility under subsection 37(1) and Investment Tax Credit eligibility.

A parallel statutory bar governs the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit under paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the ITA. Paragraph 127(9)(m) provides that no amount may be included in computing a taxpayer's investment tax credit in respect of a qualified expenditure if the taxpayer does not file with the Minister a prescribed form containing prescribed information in respect of the amount (specifically Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations, or Form T2038(IND) for individuals) on or before the day that is one year after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the particular taxation year. Furthermore, as confirmed by the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy and Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence including the later decision in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. (2017 TCC 9, Docket: 2015-3982(IT)G, affirmed 2018 FCA 57) and the earlier decision in Alcatel Canada Inc. (2005 TCC), all information requested on Form T661 and its supporting schedules constitutes "prescribed information". Specifically, Part 2 of Form T661 (Project Information, encompassing Sections A to C and boxes 240, 242, and 244/246) requires a complete technical narrative for each project claimed, detailing the scientific or technological uncertainties, the systematic investigation performed in the taxation year, and the resulting advancements. Prescribed information also encompasses mandatory supporting schedules where applicable, including Forms T1145, T1146, T1174, and T1263, as well as Schedule T2SCH49 in support of Schedule T2SCH31, and claim preparer information under paragraph 37(11)(b) and subsection 162(5.3).
The Court's Final Holding

In his Reasons for Judgment rendered on October 14, 2009, Justice E.A. Bowie dismissed the appeal from the reassessment made under the Income Tax Act for the 2005 taxation year. Evaluating the oral testimony of the Appellant's three witnesses (Benjamin Mair, Kevin Wong, and Blair Mabee) against the physical documentary exhibits and the institutional evidence adduced by the Respondent's witness (CRA Sudbury Appeals Officer Christine Lockwood), Justice Bowie concluded on a balance of probabilities that the technical report was not filed by the Appellant or its representative on March 28, 2007. Instead, the Court found that the technical report was only submitted after the CRA assessor's telephone call on April 10, 2007, and therefore beyond the March 31, 2007 statutory deadline for the 2005 taxation year. Emphasizing that the Appellant bore the legal onus of proving that its prescribed information was timely filed, Justice Bowie held that the Appellant's evidence fell short of discharging that burden.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures

A comprehensive legal and technical deconstruction of One Source Metal demonstrates that the loss of the Appellant's 2005 SR&ED claim resulted from an intersecting chain of legal, administrative, contractual, and evidentiary failures. Rather than turning on any substantive dispute over the underlying R&D work (whose nature the Reasons do not describe), the disqualification arose from six critical compliance breakdowns that rendered the substantive merits of the R&D project legally irrelevant.
1. Statutory Severance of Financial Schedules from Prescribed Technical Project Information

The foundational legal failure in One Source Metal was the submission of Form T661 and Schedule 31 on March 28, 2007, without the accompanying technical project report. In Canadian SR&ED practice, taxpayers and general practice accountants occasionally operate under the mistaken belief that filing the financial pages of Form T661 and Schedule 31 before the 12-month reporting deadline is sufficient to "protect" the filing date, assuming the technical project narratives can be supplied later upon request by a CRA reviewer.

Both One Source Metal (2009 TCC 511)—in which the parties agreed that both the T661 and the technical report had to be filed by the deadline, and the Court applied subsection 37(11) alone—and subsequent Tax Court of Canada decisions such as Westsource Group Holdings Inc. (2017 TCC 9) illustrate that this assumption is fatal under subsection 37(11) (and, under the current legislation, subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12)) of the ITA. The instructions on Form T661 explicitly state that the information requested in the form and documents supporting the expenditures are "prescribed information". As emphasized in Westsource, where Justice V.A. Miller adopted the submission of counsel for the Respondent, the information required in boxes 240, 242 and 244 of Form T661 "goes to the heart of whether the claim made is SR&ED". Without the prescribed technical narrative describing the technological obstacles or uncertainties and the systematic investigation performed during the taxation year, the Form T661 is legally incomplete. Under the current subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12), an incomplete form that omits the technical narrative is treated identically to an unfiled form; in One Source Metal itself, however, the Court did not refer to subsection 37(11.1) (which did not then exist) or to subsection 37(12), but simply held that, because the technical report was not filed until after April 10, 2007, the 2005 claim was not filed within the time required by subsection 37(11), and dismissed the appeal—the Reasons do not discuss any discretion to excuse the late filing.
2. Multi-Party Advisory Fragmentation and Absence of Unitary Filing Ownership

A primary operational catalyst for the missing technical report in One Source Metal was the uncoordinated division of responsibilities across three distinct parties: the Appellant's principal (Benjamin Mair), the specialized technical consulting firm (Business Improvement Group), and the external accounting firm (Martyn, Dooley and Partners, LLP); at the hearing, the Appellant itself was represented by its agent, Bill Hutchings, whose professional affiliation the Reasons do not state. In the Canadian SR&ED ecosystem, filing deadlines frequently fail in the gap between an external technical consultant who prepares the project narratives and an external accounting firm that prepares the corporate tax schedules.

In One Source Metal, this multi-party fragmentation created three points of failure along the chain of custody. First, Business Improvement Group prepared the technical report and Mr. Wong received it from that firm; the Reasons say nothing about any involvement by Business Improvement Group in how the report was assembled into, or delivered with, the filing package. Second, Mr. Mair attended the accounting firm's office on March 27, 2007, signed the SR&ED claims, and left the documents with the accountants to be filed; he was given file copies of the documents only at some later time. Consequently, Mr. Mair, the first of the Appellant's three witnesses, testified that he had no direct knowledge of the circumstances surrounding the actual filing. Third, within the accounting firm itself, the assembly of the documents by accountant Kevin Wong was separated from the physical counter delivery performed by employee Blair Mabee. Because no single professional owned end-to-end verification from technical narrative compilation through counter date-stamping, the omission of the technical report went entirely undetected until the CRA assessor telephoned on April 10, 2007.
3. Defective Physical Document Assembly and Multi-Year Technical Conflation

The manner in which the Appellant's accounting firm assembled the physical filing package introduced severe documentary vulnerability. Mr. Wong testified that he received a single technical report from Business Improvement Group which, in the words of the Reasons, "is common to the two years" (2005 and 2006). To prepare the submission for the Toronto West Tax Services Office, Mr. Wong stapled the 2005 Form T661 and its schedules together, stapled the 2006 Form T661 and its schedules together, and stapled the pages of the shared technical report together as a third separate unit. He then merely paper-clipped the three stapled units together without placing them inside an envelope.

This assembly practice suffered from two distinct technical and procedural flaws. First, from a document-control perspective, joining two separate corporate tax year claims and a standalone technical report with a single loose paper clip, unenclosed in an envelope (the Reasons make no mention of any transmittal cover letter), invited physical separation or clerical omission prior to delivery. Second, from a substantive SR&ED compliance perspective, relying on a single standalone technical report "common to the two years" rather than embedding a dedicated, year-specific Part 2 technical narrative directly inside the 2005 Form T661 and a separate 2006 Part 2 narrative inside the 2006 Form T661 may be criticized as inconsistent with the annual, year-specific nature of SR&ED reporting under section 37, although the Court made no finding on this point and did not treat the shared report as a ground for denying the claim. Form T661 requires the claimant to describe the systematic investigation performed in the taxation year to overcome the technological uncertainties. Had the 2005 technical project descriptions been integrated directly into Part 2 of the 2005 Form T661 and stapled as a single indivisible booklet, it would have been physically impossible for the courier to deliver and obtain a stamp on the 2005 T661 without simultaneously filing the 2005 technical report.
4. Fatal Evidentiary Contradiction in the Date-Stamped File Copies

In tax litigation before the Tax Court of Canada, the taxpayer bears the burden of demolishing the Minister's assumptions of fact on a balance of probabilities. In One Source Metal, the decisive evidentiary failure lay in the physical exhibits entered into evidence by the Appellant itself, compounded by the unreliable testimony of the courier witness, Blair Mabee.

Mr. Mabee testified that Mr. Wong gave him two sets of documents—one stamped "federal copy" and one stamped "file copy"—with explicit instructions to file the "federal copy" at the CRA Toronto West Tax Services Office and to obtain an official CRA date stamp on the "file copy" upon delivery. However, under examination, Mr. Mabee admitted that he could not remember how many documents were clipped together, offering only the sweeping assertion that all the documents he was given were delivered to the CRA. When the Appellant entered its retained "file copies" into evidence, a glaring discrepancy emerged across the three exhibits: Exhibit A-1 (the file copy of the 2005 Form T661 and schedules) and Exhibit A-2 (the file copy of the 2006 Form T661 and schedules) were both stamped "RECEIVED 2007-03-28" on their front pages, whereas Exhibit A-3 (the file copy of the technical report) contained no "received" stamp at all.

Attempting to rationalize why Exhibit A-3 bore no stamp, Mr. Mabee testified that the CRA "usually just stamps the front copy" of a document received and does not inspect the document. Justice Bowie did not accept this explanation, identifying the absence of a "received" stamp on the file copy of the technical report as the most important element in the evidence. He observed that Mr. Mabee knew that he should get a "received" stamp on the documents he filed, and that he did so for the two T661 forms. The fact that two separate stapled documents (Exhibits A-1 and A-2) were each stamped "RECEIVED 2007-03-28" while Exhibit A-3 bore no stamp at all therefore weighed heavily against the Appellant's position that the technical report was filed on March 28, 2007. Finding that Mr. Mabee "was not an impressive witness" and "had no idea how many documents he actually filed on March 28, 2007," Justice Bowie concluded it was highly improbable that Mr. Mabee would have delivered three documents while obtaining "received" stamps on only two.
5. Failure to Overcome CRA Vault Chain-of-Custody and Provincial Cross-Verification Evidence

The Reasons do not record the Appellant as having advanced a specific theory on this point, but the Respondent's evidence addressed the possibility that the technical report had been delivered on March 28, 2007, alongside the two T661 forms, but had become detached after filing and could not be matched to the Appellant's tax file because the technical report bore at the top of page one the abbreviated name under which the Appellant carried on business, "One Source Metal," rather than the corporate legal name 1373744 Ontario Inc.

The Crown addressed this possibility through the testimony of Christine Lockwood, an appeals officer in the Sudbury office of the CRA. First, Ms. Lockwood established the strict institutional chain of custody governing SR&ED claims: unlike general correspondence, SR&ED claims are accorded special handling by the CRA. Immediately upon filing at a local Tax Services Office, all SR&ED claims are transmitted directly to the Sudbury office, where they are logged by a special services clerk and stored inside a dedicated secure vault, from which they are removed only for evaluation by an assessor or, following an objection, by an appeals officer. Second, Ms. Lockwood proved that entering the trade name "One Source Metal" into the CRA's computer database directly links to the corporate entity 1373744 Ontario Inc. Consequently, even if the technical report had detached from the T661 forms after filing, the mailroom staff in Toronto, or the special services clerk in Sudbury, would have been able to associate it with the correct file. Third, Ms. Lockwood testified that her technical advisor accessed the Ontario Revenue Department's computer system, which digitally scans all provincial SR&ED applications immediately upon filing. That inter-governmental audit revealed that the Appellant's technical report had been filed with the Ontario provincial authority on April 13, 2007—three days after the CRA assessor's April 10, 2007 telephone call notifying the Appellant's representative that the technical report was missing, and one day after the date on which, according to the Respondent, the report was first filed with the CRA by fax (April 12, 2007). This objective digital timestamp from the provincial revenue authority was one of a number of elements in the evidence supporting the Court's conclusion that the technical report was not filed by the Appellant or its representative until after the assessor's telephone call on April 10, 2007.
6. Total Preclusion of Substantive Technical Review on the Merits

The overarching legal lesson of One Source Metal is that a procedural failure under subsection 37(11) completely forecloses judicial evaluation of the substantive technical eligibility of the claim under subsection 37(1) and subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Because the Court found that the technical report was not filed within the time required by subsection 37(11), it dismissed the appeal on that basis alone (without referring to subsection 37(12)), and the Tax Court of Canada never reached the questions of whether One Source Metal faced genuine technological uncertainty (the Reasons do not describe the nature of the underlying work), whether it formulated and tested hypotheses through a structured process of experimentation, or whether it maintained contemporaneous shop-floor documentation. In Canadian SR&ED law, procedural completeness of the prescribed Form T661 prior to the 12-month bar date is an absolute jurisdictional gateway; failure at that gateway destroys the claim regardless of the underlying scientific achievement.
Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and evidentiary requirement analyzed in One Source Metal (and its governing Canadian legislative provisions) against the taxpayer's specific compliance failure and the standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in One Source Metal
Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Holding

cells: Timely Filing of Prescribed Form
Income Tax Act (ITA) s. 37(11); parallel ITC rule in ITA s. 127(9) definition of "investment tax credit" para. (m); corporate filing-due date under ITA s. 150(1)(a).

While the 2005 Form T661 and Schedule 31 were delivered on March 28, 2007 (three days before the March 31, 2007 statutory deadline), the Court found that the technical report was not filed until after April 10, 2007 (according to the Respondent, it was first filed by fax on April 12, 2007).

Strict Statutory Compliance (No Equitable Discretion): The 12-month deadline after the T2 filing-due date is an absolute statutory bar. The Reasons do not discuss any power to grant extensions or to forgive late filings; the Court simply applied subsection 37(11) as written and dismissed the appeal.
Inclusion of Complete "Prescribed Information" (Technical Report / Part 2 Narratives)
ITA ss. 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12); Form T661 Part 2 (Project Information Lines 240, 242, 244); One Source Metal (2009 TCC 511); Westsource Group Holdings Inc. (2017 TCC 9).

The technical report prepared by Business Improvement Group was a separate document from the 2005 T661 (as was common ground, the claim consisted of two documents: the T661 with its schedules, and the technical report). Failed to file the technical report with the T661 by March 31, 2007; the Court found it was not filed until after April 10, 2007.

Completeness as a Substantive Condition Precedent: Both Form T661 and the technical project report must be filed before the deadline. In One Source Metal this requirement was common ground and the Court applied subsection 37(11) alone; under the current ss. 37(11.1) and 37(12) (s. 37(11.1) having been enacted after the decision), omitting prescribed technical information deems the claimed expenditures not to be SR&ED expenditures at all.
Verifiable Proof of Delivery & Receipt by the Minister
Common law burden of proof in tax appeals; Tax Court of Canada Rules (Informal Procedure), under which this appeal (Docket 2008-3566(IT)I) was heard; One Source Metal (2009 TCC 511) paras. 6, 10.

Retained a "file copy" of the 2005 T661 (Exhibit A-1) and 2006 T661 (Exhibit A-2) bearing CRA "RECEIVED 2007-03-28" stamps, but produced an unstamped "file copy" of the technical report (Exhibit A-3).

Balance of Probabilities Anchored in Objective Documentary Proof: The taxpayer bears the onus of proving timely receipt. The Court did not lay down a rule that every document must bear a stamp, but treated the absence of a "received" stamp on the file copy of the technical report as the most important element of the evidence; prudence therefore dictates that, where multiple documents are filed together via hand-delivery, every distinct document file copy bear an official CRA date-received stamp (or modern electronic confirmation receipt listing all transmitted schedules).
Credible Witness Testimony & Chain of Custody from Preparer to CRA
Principles of viva voce evidence and witness credibility in the Tax Court of Canada; One Source Metal (2009 TCC 511) paras. 3–6, 10.

The company principal (Mr. Mair) had no personal knowledge of filing. The accountant (Mr. Wong) merely paper-clipped three stapled units without an envelope. The runner (Mr. Mabee) could not recall how many documents were clipped together and offered an explanation of CRA stamping practices that the Court did not accept.

Strict Scrutiny of Vague or Self-Serving Recollection: The Court found that Mr. Mabee was not an impressive witness, that he had no idea how many documents he actually filed, and that his assertion that all the documents he was given were delivered to the CRA did not overcome the physical exhibits. The Court considered it most unlikely that he would have filed three documents and had only two copies stamped "received".
Rebuttal of Institutional CRA Logging & Provincial Cross-Checks
CRA Sudbury Tax Centre SR&ED vault logging protocols; CRA computer system trade-name indexing; Provincial SR&ED digital scanning logs; One Source Metal paras. 7–10.

The Respondent's evidence addressed the possibility (not recorded in the Reasons as a theory advanced by the Appellant) that the paper-clipped technical report had detached after filing and could not be matched because it bore the trade name "One Source Metal" rather than 1373744 Ontario Inc.

Cumulative Evidentiary Weighing: Credible evidence of CRA's secure Sudbury vault logging, automated trade-name-to-numbered-company resolution, and provincial revenue scan logs showing an April 13, 2007 filing date were among a number of elements in the evidence supporting the Court's conclusion, although the Court did not refer to any presumption of regularity and identified the absence of a "received" stamp on the technical report as the most important element.
Year-Specific Technical Project Attribution
ITA ss. 37(1), 37(11), 249(1); Form T661 Part 2 instructions requiring description of work performed in the taxation year.
Relied on a single, unsegregated technical report "common to the two years" (2005 and 2006) prepared by an external consultant, clipped loosely to two separate annual T661 returns.

Strict Annual Periodicity: Not addressed by the Court (the Reasons merely note that the technical report was common to the two years); under current CRA requirements, each taxation year's Form T661 must contain a self-contained Part 2 technical narrative specifically isolating the technological uncertainties addressed and systematic investigation executed within that discrete fiscal period.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To demonstrate how Canadian corporate claimants and their tax advisors can systematically overcome the legal, contractual, and evidentiary pitfalls identified in One Source Metal (2009 TCC 511)—as well as related Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence on prescribed information in Westsource Group Holdings Inc. (2017 TCC 9) and Alcatel Canada Inc. (2005 TCC)—the following two detailed industry case studies examine realistic R&D projects vulnerable to summary disallowance. Each case study sets out a comprehensive, step-by-step remediation architecture covering project governance, technical documentation, contractual terms, and experimentation tracking.
Case Study 1: Advanced Metallurgical and Progressive Die Stamping Manufacturer (Multi-Year Claim with Bifurcated External Advisors)
Industry Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

Apex Precision Stamping Inc. ("Apex"), an Ontario-incorporated Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) operating under the registered trade name "Apex Metalworks", manufactures high-tolerance structural automotive chassis stampings in Mississauga, Ontario. Apex has a corporate fiscal year-end of September 30. Across its 2024 and 2025 taxation years (spanning October 1, 2023, to September 30, 2025), Apex executed a major experimental development project titled Project 24-01: Cold-Forming Micro-Alloyed Ultra-High-Strength Steel (UHSS) Without Hydrogen-Induced Delayed Cracking.

Apex's compliance workflow replicates the exact vulnerabilities that proved fatal in One Source Metal. Having postponed the preparation of its 2024 SR&ED claim until late March 2026—mere days before its March 31, 2026 statutory 18-month reporting deadline for the September 30, 2024 taxation year—Apex's Vice President of Finance decides to bundle and submit the 2024 and 2025 SR&ED claims simultaneously. To expedite preparation, Apex retains a boutique SR&ED engineering consultancy ("TechGrant Advisors") on a contingent-fee basis to write the technical project narrative, while relying on its external Chartered Professional Accountant (CPA) firm to prepare the T2 corporate return amendments, the financial sections of Form T661, Schedule T2SCH31, and Ontario Schedule 508 (Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit). TechGrant Advisors drafts a single, continuous 18-page Word document titled "Apex Metalworks – 2024/2025 SR&ED Technical Report" that blends metallurgical trials from November 2023 through August 2025 without segregating which hypotheses and tests occurred in the 2024 fiscal year versus the 2025 fiscal year, and displays only the trade name "Apex Metalworks" rather than the numbered/corporate legal name Apex Precision Stamping Inc. Three days before March 31, 2026, TechGrant Advisors emails the Word file to the CPA firm. A junior accountant keys the financial expenditure figures into the tax software for the 2024 and 2025 Forms T661, inserts the phrase "See attached technical report" into Part 2 (Lines 242, 244, and 246), and submits an amended filing package in which the standalone technical report is either omitted from the electronic XML transmission or left unstamped during counter delivery. Under One Source Metal and Westsource Group Holdings Inc., Apex faces the complete loss of its $680,000 FY2024 SR&ED expenditure deduction and over $250,000 in combined federal and provincial ITCs under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12) of the ITA.
Step 1: Project Governance and Filing Chain-of-Custody Restructuring

To eliminate the One Source Metal delivery and verification breakdown, Apex must replace last-minute 18-month brinkmanship with a formal SR&ED Statutory Filing Protocol anchored to its regular corporate tax return cycle. Following the explicit recommendation in the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, Apex must mandate as a matter of corporate governance that Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 be filed concurrently with its original T2 corporate income tax return on or before the six-month corporate filing-due date under paragraph 150(1)(a) (March 31 following its September 30 fiscal year-end), utilizing the remaining 12-month statutory window under subsection 37(11) strictly as a safety buffer for audited financial or technical adjustments.

Furthermore, Apex's governance policy must strictly prohibit the creation or submission of detached, standalone Word or PDF "technical reports". Instead, all Part 2 project narratives must be directly populated into the certified T2 tax preparation software fields (Lines 242, 244, and 246 of Form T661) so that the technical project descriptions are embedded inside the single unified XML transmission dispatched via CRA Corporation Internet Filing (CIF) directly into the CRA's CORTAX system. In the event any supplementary schedule or paper submission is ever delivered in person to a CRA Tax Services Office or uploaded via the CRA "Submit Documents" portal, Apex's Controller must execute a mandatory Pre-Filing Chain-of-Custody Protocol: every single page must carry a header displaying the exact corporate legal name (Apex Precision Stamping Inc.), the trade name (o/a Apex Metalworks), the 9-digit Business Number (BN) and RC account identifier, the specific taxation year-end, and continuous pagination (Page X of Y). If delivered physically at a CRA counter, the submission must be bound as a single inseparable booklet per taxation year, accompanied by an itemized Transmittal Cover Letter listing every enclosed form and page count, and the designated courier must be instructed in writing not to leave the CRA counter until the receiving officer applies an official "RECEIVED" date stamp to the file copy of the Transmittal Cover Letter, the front page of Form T661, and the first page of Part 2.
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Fiscal-Year Segregation

To cure the fatal defect of a blended multi-year technical report and satisfy both the procedural mandate of subsection 37(11) and the substantive criteria of subsection 248(1) of the ITA, Apex must segregate its technical narratives strictly by taxation year and map them directly into the prescribed boxes of Part 2 of Form T661. For the 2024 taxation year (October 1, 2023, to September 30, 2024), Apex's Metallurgical Engineering Lead must draft a dedicated Part 2 narrative restricted exclusively to the technological uncertainties and experimental trials conducted prior to September 30, 2024.

In Line 242 (Scientific or Technological Uncertainties – Maximum 350 Words) of the 2024 Form T661, Apex must distinguish its metallurgical system uncertainty from routine die tryout or tooling adjustment. Specifically, the narrative must explain that existing forming limit diagrams (FLDs) and finite element simulations could not predict localized martensitic phase transformation and hydrogen-assisted micro-void coalescence at bend radii below 2.0 times the sheet thickness when cold-stamping 1,200 MPa dual-phase micro-alloyed steel at progressive press speeds exceeding 45 strokes per minute, due to non-linear interaction between adiabatic shear heating and residual tensile stress gradients.

In Line 244 (Work Performed in the Tax Year to Overcome the Technological Obstacles/Uncertainties – Maximum 700 Words) of the 2024 Form T661, Apex must document only the systematic investigation executed between October 1, 2023, and September 30, 2024. The text must articulate a structured sequence of hypotheses, experimental configurations, and quantitative analytical results—specifically detailing FY2024 Test Series 1 through 4, where engineers systematically varied vanadium-niobium micro-alloy chemistries, servo-press slide velocity deceleration curves, and physical vapour deposition (PVD) die coatings across 16 instrumented coil runs, measuring retained austenite Transformation-Induced Plasticity (TRIP) effects via X-ray diffraction and scanning electron microscopy. Crucially, all subsequent experimental trials conducted on or after October 1, 2024 (such as FY2025 Test Series 5 through 8 involving sub-zero induction temper relief) must be completely excluded from the 2024 Form T661 and documented exclusively in Line 244 of the 2025 Form T661.

In Line 246 (Scientific or Technological Advancements Achieved – Maximum 350 Words) of the 2024 Form T661, Apex must articulate the specific incremental advancement in metallurgical engineering knowledge achieved as of September 30, 2024—namely, establishing the quantitative empirical correlation between adiabatic interface temperatures exceeding 180 °C and grain-boundary decohesion in Nb-Ti micro-alloyed UHSS—even though the commercial tooling only achieved full production validation in FY2025.
Step 3: Tripartite Contractual Terms and Statutory Preparer Accountability

In One Source Metal, the Appellant suffered total disallowance because its external technical consultant and external accounting firm operated in silos without contractual accountability for the integrated filing. Moreover, under paragraph 37(11)(b) and subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3) of the ITA, failing to accurately report "claim preparer information" on Form T661 exposes both the taxpayer and the claim preparer to joint and several statutory penalties.

To eliminate this contractual gap, Apex must replace separate bilateral engagement letters with a unified Tripartite SR&ED Preparation and Filing Agreement executed by Apex, TechGrant Advisors, and the external CPA firm. This contract must designate a single named tax partner at the CPA firm as the Statutory Filing Owner, legally responsible for compiling and transmitting the complete T2, Form T661 (including Part 2), Schedule T2SCH31, and provincial Schedule 508. Simultaneously, the contract must obligate the lead engineering advisor at TechGrant Advisors to inspect and countersign the final compiled tax software printout (and XML validation log) prior to transmission, certifying in writing that Lines 242, 244, and 246 of Part 2 are fully populated within the electronic file. The agreement must also require both advisory firms to provide their complete statutory identification, preparer numbers, and billing arrangements for mandatory disclosure in Part 9 (Claim Preparer Information) of Form T661 pursuant to paragraph 37(11)(b) and subsection 162(5.3), coupled with an indemnification and fee-forfeiture clause stipulating that no contingency or preparation fee is payable if any portion of the claim is disallowed under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), or 37(12) due to late or incomplete filing of prescribed information.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Experimentation and Financial Tracking

To ensure that once the procedural threshold of subsection 37(11) is satisfied, Apex's claim passes substantive CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer scrutiny, Apex must synchronize its shop-floor experimentation tracking with Form T661 Section C (Lines 270–279) and Part 3 expenditure rules. Apex must configure its Manufacturing Execution System (MES) to generate dedicated SR&ED Experimental Trial Tickets whenever the press line is taken offline for experimental runs. Each ticket must contemporaneously record the date, the specific hypothesis from Line 244 being tested, the coil heat lot number and mass of steel consumed or transformed into scrap under Form T661 Line 320/325, the exact press hours logged by metallurgical engineers and tool-and-die makers, and the resulting laboratory tensile and metallographic test reports.

cells: Filing Timeline & Delivery
Filing 3 days before the 18-month bar date via loose paper-clipped bundles.
Concurrent filing with the T2 return at 6 months post-year-end via encrypted CRA CIF/CORTAX XML transmission.
Technical Report Integration
Standalone report "common to the two years" (2005 and 2006), filed as a document separate from Form T661.
Direct character-validated entry into Part 2 (Lines 242, 244, 246) inside each respective year's T661 XML schema.
Entity & Fiscal Period Attribution
Trade name (rather than corporate name) at the top of page one of the report; a single technical report common to two taxation years.
Full corporate legal name, BN, and strict October 1 – September 30 fiscal cutoff on every project schedule.
Advisory Governance
Uncoordinated handoffs between technical consultant, accountant, and runner.
Tripartite contract naming a single Statutory Filing Owner, mandatory pre-transmission XML sign-off, and Part 9 preparer disclosure under ITA s. 37(11)(b).

body.text: Case Study 2: Industrial Automation and Embedded Robotics Integrator (High-Volume Multi-Project Claimant with Subcontracted R&D)
Industry Scenario and Vulnerability Profile

Vectra Robotics & Control Corp. ("Vectra"), a mid-sized Canadian engineering corporation headquartered in Waterloo, Ontario, with R&D centres in Ontario and Quebec, develops autonomous 3D vision-guided robotic laser welding and non-destructive inspection cells. Vectra executes approximately 28 concurrent experimental development projects per taxation year and engages both arm's length Canadian subcontractors (under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) of the ITA) and non-arm's length affiliate engineering entities to perform specialized electromagnetic interference (EMI) attenuation testing and custom photonic sensor fabrication.

Vectra confronts a sophisticated, high-volume manifestation of the One Source Metal and Westsource Group Holdings Inc. prescribed-information trap. Facing intense time pressure as its 12-month reporting deadline under subsection 37(11) approaches, Vectra's internal tax manager—operating under an erroneous belief that claimants with more than 20 projects only need to submit technical descriptions for their largest 20 projects—files a Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 claiming $4.2 million in qualified SR&ED expenditures across all 28 projects in Part 3 and Part 4, but includes Part 2 technical project descriptions (Sections A, B, and C) for only the top 18 projects, planning to hand the remaining 10 project narratives to the CRA Research and Technology Advisor during the audit. Furthermore, Vectra claims related-party R&D transfers and university research contract payments on Form T661 without filing the mandatory supporting prescribed forms—specifically Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), and Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED)—before the reporting deadline. Finally, Vectra submits its federal T661 and its provincial claims (Ontario Schedule 508 and Revenu Québec Form RD-222) on staggered dates with mismatched project lists, creating an inter-governmental audit trail of the kind that was used as evidence against the taxpayer in One Source Metal.

Under subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12) of the ITA, as applied (in the case of One Source Metal, through subsection 37(11) only) by the Tax Court of Canada in One Source Metal and Westsource Group Holdings Inc. and codified in the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, Vectra's omission of Part 2 narratives for Projects 19 through 28 by the statutory reporting deadline is legally fatal to those 10 projects. As CRA policy explicitly dictates, where a claimant provides prescribed project information for only a subset of its claimed projects by the reporting deadline, the CRA will accept only the documented projects as meeting the statutory filing requirements, and will permanently disallow all expenditures and ITCs attributable to the undescribed projects pursuant to subsections 37(11.1) and 37(12). Similarly, omitting prescribed supporting forms such as Forms T1145, T1146, and T1263 invalidates the associated expenditure claims.
Step 1: Project Governance and Digital CORTAX Submission Verification

To insulate its multi-project portfolio against partial or total disqualification under subsections 37(11) and 37(11.1), Vectra must institute a strict Project-to-Expenditure Parity Gate within its corporate tax governance framework. First, Vectra must abandon the misconception that Part 2 narratives can be selectively filed for only the top 20 projects; CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy unambiguously mandates that a separate, complete Part 2 (Sections A to C) is required for every single project claimed on Form T661 on or before the 12-month reporting deadline.

To make this manageable without sacrificing eligible expenditures, Vectra's Vice President of Engineering must restructure project taxonomy at the beginning of each fiscal year by grouping commercial customer work orders around the core underlying scientific or technological uncertainties they share, legitimately consolidating 28 fragmented commercial tickets into 10 to 12 overarching, multi-disciplinary SR&ED programs. Second, Vectra's financial ERP and tax software must enforce a hard programmatic lock: no dollar of salary, material, overhead proxy, or subcontractor cost may be summed into Part 3 (Lines 300 to 570) of Form T661 unless its parent Project ID has a 100% populated Part 2 (Lines 200 through 279) verified in the CORTAX XML pre-transmission audit. Third, Vectra must synchronize its federal CRA filing and its provincial filings (Ontario Schedule 508 and Revenu Québec RD-222/RD-1029.7) to occur on the exact same business day, archiving a complete cryptographic hash and PDF rendering of the transmitted package to prevent any inter-jurisdictional date discrepancy of the kind exposed by CRA Appeals Officer Christine Lockwood in One Source Metal.
Step 2: Technical Documentation Architecture (Complete Project-by-Project Part 2 Narratives)

To eliminate the year-end administrative bottleneck that tempts claimants to omit smaller Part 2 project narratives, Vectra must transition from retrospective post-year-end report writing to a Quarterly Rolling Part 2 Technical Dossier workflow. Because waiting up to 18 months after the fiscal year-end allows key robotics and firmware engineers to leave the company—destroying institutional memory and witness credibility at the Tax Court of Canada—Vectra's project managers must draft and update Part 2 Sections A, B, and C at the close of each fiscal quarter.

For each consolidated SR&ED project, the Quarterly Technical Dossier must enforce complete population of all prescribed Part 2 fields required by the CRA: Section A (Project Identification, including project title on Line 200, internal code on Line 202, start and completion dates on Lines 204–206, field of science or technology code on Line 208, and continuation status on Line 210); Section B (Project Descriptions on Lines 242, 244, and 246); and Section C (Additional Project Information, including key technical personnel on Lines 260–269 and contemporaneous documentation checkboxes on Lines 270–279). In drafting Line 242 and Line 244 for its autonomous robotic welding cells, Vectra's engineers must carefully separate routine commercial systems integration and CAD customization from genuine technological uncertainty—such as overcoming real-time chromatic aberration and specular laser reflection noise in multi-spectral CMOS seam-tracking algorithms operating within high-density plasma arc plumes.
Step 3: Contractual Terms for Subcontractors, Affiliates, and Third-Party Payments

Because the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy explicitly defines "prescribed information" under subsection 37(11) to include all supporting schedules and agreements required to substantiate Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31—specifically naming Forms T1145, T1146, T1174, and T1263, and Schedule T2SCH49—Vectra must overhaul both its external subcontractor contracts and its intercompany R&D agreements.

For arm's length Canadian subcontractors performing EMI testing and sensor board prototyping under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) of the ITA, Vectra's Master Services Agreements (MSAs) and Statements of Work (SOWs) must include four mandatory SR&ED clauses: first, an explicit statement that the subcontractor is performing SR&ED directly on behalf of Vectra within Canada; second, an intellectual property covenant confirming that Vectra retains sole ownership and the exclusive right to exploit all resulting SR&ED outputs; third, a billing covenant requiring the subcontractor to segregate eligible Canadian SR&ED engineering labour and consumed materials from commercial production or foreign activities on every invoice (supporting the 80% qualified expenditure inclusion under subparagraph 127(9)(a)(ii)); and fourth, a mandatory deliverable schedule requiring the subcontractor to deliver raw experimental test data and failure logs to Vectra at least 30 days prior to fiscal year-end so those experiments can be incorporated into Vectra's Line 244 narrative. For non-arm's length R&D contracts and third-party payments to approved universities or research institutes under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(ii), Vectra's intercompany and institutional agreements must mandate that the counterparties execute Form T1145, Form T1146, or Form T1263 within 90 days of fiscal year-end, ensuring that those prescribed forms are electronically transmitted alongside Form T661 well ahead of the subsection 37(11) bar date.
Step 4: Systematic Experimentation and Time-Tracking Audit Trails

Finally, to substantiate the link between its timely filed Part 2 project narratives and its Part 3 financial expenditures during a joint CRA technical and financial review, Vectra must integrate its software and hardware engineering repositories directly with its time-tracking and general ledger systems. All experimental firmware commits in Git, issue tickets in Jira, and hardware revision logs in the Product Lifecycle Management (PLM) database must be tagged with a mandatory metadata prefix corresponding to the specific Form T661 Project Code (Line 202) and the specific Hypothesis ID described in Line 244. Concurrently, all R&D personnel—including non-arm's length specified employees subject to salary and proxy caps—must complete bi-weekly contemporaneous timesheets allocating their hours by Project Code and Hypothesis ID, supported by automated commit logs.

headers: Pre-Remediation Vulnerability (One Source Metal & Westsource Pitfall)

cells: Multi-Project Part 2 Completeness
Claiming expenditures for 28 projects on Part 3 while filing Part 2 narratives for only 18 projects by the deadline.
Consolidating related tickets by core technological uncertainty and enforcing a 100% ERP lock requiring a complete Part 2 for every claimed Project ID.
Prescribed Supporting Schedules
Omitting Forms T1145, T1146, and T1263 at the time of T661 filing.
Contractual covenants requiring counterparty execution of Forms T1145, T1146, and T1263 within 90 days of year-end for simultaneous CIF transmission.
Inter-Governmental Consistency
Staggered federal (CRA) and provincial (Ontario/Quebec) filings with mismatched project narratives.
Simultaneous same-day electronic transmission of federal T2/T661/T2SCH31 and provincial schedules with identical timestamped project dossiers.
Subcontractor & Labour Substantiation
Unsegregated subcontractor invoices and retrospective year-end time estimates.
MSA clauses mandating Canadian SR&ED cost segregation under ITA s. 37(1)(a)(i.01) and bi-weekly timesheets linked to Git/Jira hypothesis tags.

body.text: Synthesis and Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in 1373744 Ontario Inc. o/a One Source Metal v. Her Majesty the Queen (2009 TCC 511) remains an essential cautionary decision (albeit one rendered under the Informal Procedure and therefore without precedential value) for Canadian corporate taxpayers, tax counsel, Chartered Professional Accountants, and technical SR&ED advisors. The ruling, which applied subsection 37(11), underscores that the statutory filing requirements now found in subsections 37(11), 37(11.1), and 37(12) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act are not flexible administrative guidelines, but strict substantive preconditions to tax deductibility and Investment Tax Credit entitlement. By embedding technical narratives directly into Part 2 of Form T661 for every claimed project on a strictly segregated fiscal-year basis, enforcing unitary contractual accountability across external technical and accounting preparers under paragraph 37(11)(b), and preserving an unimpeachable digital or date-stamped chain of custody well ahead of the 12-month reporting deadline, Canadian claimants can completely insulate their R&D tax incentives from procedural forfeiture.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; court ruled that filing prescribed Form T661 on time is strictly mandatory to claim SR&ED credits.
